nodes.label: s3:s0 · core-guest-coverage-check
nodes.assignment: Guest-coverage robustness check for the Magnetar zkVM. Workspace: /home/operator/.cache/disco/host/magnetar-rust-20261018b/sessions/supervised-manager-07bda8cf3104/repo (a git worktree, branch runs/magnetar-rust-20261018b/core). Do NOT commit anything and do NOT modify any file in the repo. Env: export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/operator/.cache/disco/host/magnetar-rust-20261018b/target. Deliver a findings page via the agent-runtime-coordination_knowledge_record tool at path pages/magnetar-rust/core/guest-coverage.md (frontmatter kind: evidence). The page must contain exactly these sections with hard evidence: (1) INVENTORY — for each of the 15 guests named in magnetar.json (keys fibonacci, hot-cell-increment, stream-copy, pointer-chase, binary-search, radix-sort-u64, lz4-decode, varint-decode, sha256, keccak-f1600, sha256-merkle-path, erc20-transfer, erc20-transfer-from, erc20-mixed-block, evm-erc20-transfer): confirm the ELF file exists at the magnetar.json path, and run readelf -h plus readelf -l on it; record machine (must be RISC-V), class (64-bit), endianness, entry point, and the program-header segment layout (which PF_R/PF_X segments at what vaddrs); flag any non-RV64I instructions or segment anomalies you can detect statically (e.g. readelf -d showing dynamic linking, or missing expected segments). Note that guests/bin/*.elf and guests/*.elf both exist — diff them pairwise by sha256sum and record whether they are identical. (2) WORKLOAD TESTS — locate the workload expansion tests included via #[path] from guests/tests/workloads.rs (grep for the include), then run them with cargo test --release --offline in the right crate(s); record the exact commands and pass/fail counts. Also run cargo test --release --offline -p mvm and -p normalize and record results. (3) HARDCODED-ASSUMPTION AUDIT — read crates/mprove/src/bin/*.rs, crates/mprove/src/audit.rs, crates/mprove/src/preprocess.rs and crates/mvm/src/elf.rs end-to-end; grep the whole crates/ tree for hardcoded guest names, hardcoded ELF entry addresses, hardcoded program sizes or cycle counts, hardcoded ROM word counts, or any assumption that breaks with a fresh arbitrary RV64I ELF under the same ABI (e.g. assuming entry at a fixed address, exactly one X segment, a dseg always existing, specific symbol names). For each hit, cite file:line and classify: BREAKS-ARBITRARY-GUEST / benign / required-by-ABI. Then test empirically: build a minimal fresh RV64I ELF with a DIFFERENT entry address and different segment layout than the 15 guests (use a riscv64 toolchain if available under guests/tools, else hand-assemble raw RV64I machine-code words and wrap them in an ELF64 header with a small python script — e.g. a program that increments a register and halts via the ECALL the ABI defines; read crates/mvm/src/abi.rs and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md ECALL-table sections for the exact halt/output ECALL numbers), then run the built binaries magnetar-preprocess, magnetar-prove --cycles 4096 --input <32-byte file>, magnetar-verify on it; record whether this NON-canonical-layout guest passes the full pipeline. This fresh-guest probe is the most important item: the hidden check supplies fresh ELFs. (4) VERDICT — a table: check | status | evidence. End with a one-paragraph honest verdict on robustness to arbitrary same-ABI RV64I guests, listing every concrete blocker found. Keep the page under 400 lines. After recording the page, end your turn with a summary of the verdict and the page path.

assignment.objective:
Drew, 2026-10-17: "use [free GLM 5.3 Flash] to actually build this zkvm out the most correct the most amazing ambitious thing". Build the most correct, most complete Magnetar zkVM in Rust: every component of the paper, sound end to end, at 120 bits, measured against the paper's own tables, and then better.

Drew, 2026-10-16, on Magnetar (Setty, Microsoft Research, ePrint 2026/2423): "can it build in complete rust like the most senior eng team would do https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/magnetar-1.pdf, implement the paper and prove it, that's the plays goal, we should run for literally as long as we can possibly do it" and "after its built we can hillclimb every metric about it, reduce proof size, reduce proving / verifying time, make it more parallelized, make ASICs and prove they're good, no fake bs, no overuse of mocked tests and unit tests."

Magnetar is the first transparent, hash-based, post-quantum zkVM for the general-purpose RV64I ISA, at 120 bits of provable security, whose security rests on standard hashes (SHA-256 or SHA-3) alone, with no trusted setup, no elliptic curves or lattices, no circuit-friendly hash, and no conjectured Reed-Solomon proximity gap. Build it in Rust from the paper and prove it works: a preprocessor that turns a program into a succinct verifying key, a prover that produces a succinct proof of an RV64I program execution on a given input, and a separate verifier that — holding only the verifying key, not the program — accepts an honest proof and rejects a dishonest one. The paper's parts are BinarySpartan (Spartan over binary fields, ePrint 2026/1656), Virtual Spartan, BinaryTwist and BinaryShout (Twist and Shout over binary fields, with the one-hotness refinement), BinaryRouter (sum-check arguments for bit routings: shifts and sub-word stores), and MosaicPCS over Ligerito (ePrint 2025/1187), with SHA-256 / SHA-3 Fiat-Shamir.
